title: Parenting Children with Differences in Sex Development Across Developmental Stages: A Qualitative Study
content: Background: Parents of children with differences of sex development (DSD) face diagnostic uncertainty, complex decision-making, and concerns regarding long-term psychosocial outcomes. While research has examined parental experiences surrounding diagnosis, less is known about parenting across developmental stages. This study explored parents’ experiences of raising adolescents and young adults (AYAs) with DSD over time. Methods: We conducted semi-structured interviews with 11 parents of eight AYAs (16–26 years) with a range of DSD conditions, recruited through specialized services in Norway. The study was informed by phenomenological and hermeneutic perspectives, while reflexive thematic analysis was the analytic method. Results: Three themes captured parents’ long-term experiences. First, parents described variable healthcare experiences, including distress at the time of diagnosis, mixed communication, and inconsistent support during transition to adult care. Second, parents balanced openness with concerns about stigma, privacy, and their child’s autonomy. Third, parents developed coping strategies to support their child’s well-being and independence, foster a sense of normalcy and manage emotional and relational challenges over time. Conclusions: Parenting a child with DSD was an ongoing process shaped by uncertainty, stigma, and shifting relational demands. Parents’ coping was influenced by healthcare communication, continuity of care, social support, and the balance between protection and empowerment. These findings highlight the need for trauma-informed, developmentally sensitive, family-centered care that supports shared decision-making, provides guidance on disclosure, and ensures continuity into adult services.
